title: Clinical Deep Phenotyping
summary:
In the Clinical Deep Phenotyping (CDP) study, an interdisciplinary and transdiagnostic approach is used to comprehensively characterize the phenotype (features such as MRI-based imaging, electrophysiology, neuropsychology, and clinical assessment) of psychiatric patients across the spectrum of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, ADHD, autism, and anxiety disorders (including climate anxiety). This is achieved through detailed imaging, electrophysiological, and neuropsychological investigations, with the aim of combining this information with genetic analyses (genotype) to better understand the underlying dysfunctional mechanisms of severe psychiatric disorders.

The phenotype refers to the observable characteristics of an organism (morphology, physiology, behavior, etc.), while the genotype encompasses the entire genetic makeup of an organism. In the context of biological psychiatry, this means that various methods are employed to achieve the most precise possible description of an individual's characteristics (=phenotyping) and genetics (=genotyping). In phenotyping, we do not rely on traditional psychiatric diagnoses but rather on the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) developed by the National Institute of Mental Health (USA).
[Reference: https://www.nimh.nih.gov/research/research-funded-by-nimh/rdoc/index.shtml]

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Participants of the Mental Health Biobank Bonn who have consented to re-contact
- Schizophrenia spectrum disorder (ICD-10: F2X.X), bipolar affective disorder (ICD-10: F31.X), depression (ICD-10: F32.X and F33.X), ADHD (ICD-10: F90.0), autism spectrum disorder (ICD-10: F84.X), and anxiety disorder including "climate anxiety" (ICD-10: F41.X), healthy controls
Exclusion criteria:
- Patients with a primary psychiatric diagnosis other than the defined target disorders
- Age under 18 years or over 65 years
- Patients who, in the judgment of the principal investigator, are not suitable for participation in the study
- Patients presenting with acute risk of self-harm or harm to others (e.g., acutely suicidal patients)
- Patients with relevant comorbidities of the central nervous system (particularly cerebrovascular disease, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer’s dementia) or clearly organically induced psychiatric symptoms (e.g., medication-induced, metabolically caused, or infection-/delirium-related)
- Patients who are unable to provide informed consent
